meta.title: Kafka Express — learn Apache Kafka by playing
meta.description: A visual game that teaches Apache Kafka: route parcels, run partitions and keep the city's events flowing.

landing.title: Kafka Express
landing.tagline: You're the new dispatcher. Route every order onto the right conveyor and discover how Apache Kafka really works — partitions, offsets, consumers and all.

facts.visual: Watch every record travel through the factory
facts.predict: Predict what happens, then see if you were right
facts.real: Real Kafka 4.x behaviour, down to the hash function

landing.headline: Learn Kafka by running the hub.

play.title: Dispatch desk
play.missionText: The “orders” topic has 3 partitions — three belts. Send orders and find out where each one lands.

objectives.noKey: Send an order with no key
objectives.allBelts: Get a parcel onto every belt

send5.title: Offsets only go up
send5.body: Each belt stamps parcels 0, 1, 2… in arrival order. That number is the offset — its position in this partition's log.

sameKey.title: Same key → same partition
sameKey.body: murmur2(key) % partitions always gives the same belt for the same key. That's how Kafka keeps one customer's orders in order.

noKey.title: No key? Sticky partition
noKey.body: Records without a key stick to one belt until a batch fills, then switch. Fast — but no ordering guarantee across them.

allBelts.title: Partitions spread the load
allBelts.body: Different keys land on different belts, so work runs in parallel. Order is only guaranteed inside one partition.

complete.title: Shift complete!
complete.body: You've got keys, partitions and offsets. Keep dispatching — World 1 opens soon.

level.noPeeking: The factory is hidden on purpose: recalling from memory is what makes it stick.
level.remedial: You need 80% to unlock the next level. Try again: the questions change their numbers.

map.locked: Pass the previous level to unlock

w1.title: Events & the Log
w1.body: Every story in Kafka starts with a record on a log. Learn what a record is, why reading never deletes, what offsets are and how topics organize it all.

w2.title: Partitions & Keys
w2.body: Partitions are how Kafka scales, and keys are how it keeps order. Learn how to choose a partition count, why keys matter and what happens when you add partitions later.

w3.title: Producers
w3.body: How records leave the producer: batching and linger, compression, the acks that decide when a write counts as saved, and the idempotence that stops retries from creating duplicates.

sandbox.title: Free dispatch
sandbox.body: No goals, no quiz: just you, three conveyors and your customers.

shift.title: Morning shift
shift.empty: Finish a level to get your first review.
shift.due: {n, plural, one {# concept} other {# concepts}} ready for review

1-1.title: First parcel
1-1.summary: What's inside a Kafka record: key, value, headers and timestamp.

brief.title: Every event is a parcel
brief.body: Something happened (alice placed an order) and the shop wants the world to know. In Kafka that fact travels as a record. Here, each record is a parcel on its way through the hub.
brief.breaks: a real parcel can be opened and repacked. A Kafka record can’t: once it’s written, it is immutable.

pack.title: Pack your first order
pack.body: Pick a customer: their name becomes the record’s key. Toggle a header if you like, then watch the parcel leave the producer.
pack.success: Your first record is on the log!

which.q: Which part of the record decides which conveyor (partition) it goes to?
which.why: The partitioner hashes the key: murmur2(key) % partitions. Value, headers and timestamp don’t affect where it goes.

again.q: dave just landed on P{p}. Send dave again: which conveyor?
again.why: Same key, same hash, same partition: P{p}. That’s how all of one customer’s records stay in order.

more.title: Three more, one without a key
more.body: Send 3 more orders, and make at least one of them without a key. Watch where the keyless ones go.
more.success: Records without a key use sticky partitioning: they fill one conveyor for a while, then switch.

notPart.q: Which of these is NOT part of a Kafka record?
notPart.consumer: The consumer that will read it
notPart.why: A record has a key, a value, headers and a timestamp. It doesn’t know who will read it: any number of consumers can.

bytes.q: To the broker, a record’s value is…
bytes.why: Brokers store and serve bytes. Turning them into JSON, Avro or objects is the clients’ job (serializers).

timestamp.q: With the default setting (CreateTime), who sets a record’s timestamp?
timestamp.why: message.timestamp.type=CreateTime is the default: the producer stamps it. With LogAppendTime the broker does.

nullKey.q: Can a record be sent with a null key?
nullKey.yes: Yes, it’s spread with sticky partitioning
nullKey.why: Keys are optional. Keyless records stick to one partition until a batch fills, then move on, so there’s no per-key ordering.

1-2.title: The belt never forgets
1-2.summary: Reading doesn’t delete: consumers keep a position, and records are immutable.

brief.title: Reading isn’t taking
brief.body: Two teams need the orders: Billing charges customers and Shipping sends boxes. Each one is a consumer group, a robot arm that scans parcels and remembers how far it has read.
brief.breaks: in a warehouse, picking up a parcel removes it. In Kafka, reading only copies the data: the parcel stays on the belt for everyone else.

arrive.title: Orders arrive
arrive.body: The shop sends four orders to the orders topic. Both arms are waiting at offset 0.

read.q: Billing reads the record at offset 0. What happens to that parcel?
read.moves: It moves to the end of the belt
read.why: It stays exactly where it is. Billing’s flag moves to offset 1: that’s its position, the next record it will read.

catch.title: Let Shipping catch up
catch.body: Use the buttons to make Shipping read the first 3 orders. Billing’s position doesn’t change: each group keeps its own.
catch.success: Two groups, same records, independent positions.

count.q: Billing is at position {billing} and Shipping at {shipping}. How many parcels are still on the belt?
count.why: All {n} of them. Reading never deletes. Records leave the log only when retention removes old ones, which is a story for later.

change.title: Changing your mind
change.body: alice wants to change her order. You might want to edit the parcel at offset 0, but the log is append-only: records can’t be edited or moved.
change.note: to “update”, you append a new record with the same key. Consumers see both, in order, and the newest one wins.

update.q: alice changes her order. What do you do?
update.append: Append a new record with key alice
update.why: Append a new record. The old one stays, and both keep their offsets. Kafka is a history of facts, not a table you overwrite.

remain.q: A partition holds {n} records. Group Billing has read all of them. How many records are still in the partition?
remain.why: Still {n}. Reading moves the group’s position. It never removes records.

left.q: A partition has offsets 0 to {last}. Shipping’s position is {p}. How many records does Shipping still have to read?
left.why: The log holds {n} records (0…{last}). Position {p} means offsets 0…{p}−1 are done, so {left} remain.

groups.q: Two consumer groups read the same topic. Their positions are…
groups.independent: Independent: each group has its own
groups.shared: Shared: one position for the topic
groups.why: Each group tracks its own position, so many teams can read the same data at their own pace.

update.q: How do you “update” a record in Kafka?
update.append: Append a new record with the same key
update.replace: Delete it and insert at the same offset
update.why: The log is append-only and records are immutable. A new record with the same key carries the update.

1-3.title: Stamps
1-3.summary: Offsets: every partition numbers its records 0, 1, 2… on its own.

brief.title: The stamp is the offset
brief.body: When a parcel lands, its conveyor stamps it with the next number. That number is the offset: its permanent position in that partition’s log.
brief.breaks: a counter can be reset. Offsets never are. Even after old records are deleted, their numbers are never reused.

warm.title: Warming up
warm.body: Five orders roll in. Watch the stamps: each conveyor counts on its own.

nextOffset.q: {key} goes to P{p}, which already holds {c} parcels. What offset will it get?
nextOffset.why: Offsets start at 0, so a partition with {c} records has used 0…{c}−1. The next one is {c}, the log-end offset.

where.q: bob already has parcels on the line. Where will bob’s next parcel land?
where.why: Same key, same partition: P{p}. You don’t need to compute murmur2, you just need to remember where the key went before.

own.q: What offset will the next parcel on P{q} get? (It’s {key}’s conveyor.)
own.why: P{q} has its own counter: its next offset is {n}, whatever the other conveyors are at.

fill.title: Fill P1 to offset 4
fill.body: Get P1 to 5 parcels (offsets 0–4). Which customers land on P1? Experiment. You can also type any key you like.
fill.success: You found P1’s keys. Notice: P1’s offsets don’t care what P0 or P2 are doing.

last.q: P0’s next offset is {n}. You send {k} records to P0. What offset does the last one get?
last.why: They get {n}, {n}+1, … so the last is {n} + {k} − 1 = {last}.

unique.why: Every partition counts from 0, so P0 offset 3 and P1 offset 3 are different records. Offset + partition (+ topic) identify a record.

count.q: A partition holds offsets 0 to {m}. How many records is that?

position.next: The offset of the next record it will read
position.last: The offset of the last record it read
position.deleted: How many records it has deleted
position.why: Position = next offset to read. A consumer at position 5 has processed offsets 0–4.

1-4.title: Sorting docks
1-4.summary: Topics: named logs that keep different kinds of events apart.

brief.title: Each line is a topic
brief.body: The hub now handles two kinds of events: orders and payments. Each kind gets its own production line, a topic, with its own name and its own conveyors (partitions).
brief.breaks: a topic isn’t a queue. Reading doesn’t empty it, and many groups can read it at once.

route.title: Route the events
route.body: Events arrive one by one. Send each one to the right topic: orders to orders, payments to payments. Get 6 right.
route.success: Sorted! Producers always say which topic a record goes to.

cross.q: alice has an order (in orders) and a payment (in payments). Is the order between those two records guaranteed?
cross.no: No: ordering is only per partition, and these are different topics
cross.yes: Yes: they have the same key
cross.why: Kafka guarantees order within a partition. Different topics are different logs, so there’s no ordering between them, even for the same key.

cli.title: Creating a topic, for real
cli.body: Everything you’ve seen maps to real commands. This creates the payments topic with 2 partitions on a local broker. Replication comes in World 5.

count.q: How many conveyors (partitions) will this topic have?

what.log: A named log, split into partitions
what.queue: A single queue that empties as you read
what.why: A topic is a named, append-only log split into partitions. It keeps records after they’re read.

cli.q: How many partitions will this topic have?

after.q: After a consumer group reads a record from a topic, the record…
after.why: Reading never deletes. Records stay until retention (default 7 days) or compaction removes them.

order.q: Kafka guarantees the order of records…
order.why: Only within a partition. That’s why keys matter: the same key always goes to the same partition.

2-1.title: Traffic jam
2-1.summary: Partitions are the unit of parallelism: more conveyors, more workers.

brief.title: Black Friday rush
brief.body: Orders are pouring in, 2 per second. The fulfilment robot packs 1 per second per conveyor, and the orders topic has just one conveyor. Can you keep up?
brief.breaks: in Kafka you can add partitions to a live topic, but you can never remove them.

rush.title: Keep the backlog down
rush.body: Orders arrive on their own. Add conveyors until the backlog stays at 3 or less for 5 seconds.
rush.success: Backlog under control! Each new partition gave the robot one more lane to work on in parallel.

unit.title: Partitions are lanes of work
unit.body: Within a consumer group, each partition is read by at most one consumer at a time. So the partition count caps how many consumers can work in parallel. Pick it for the throughput you’ll need later, because shrinking isn’t possible.

map.consumer: One consumer per partition (in a group)

min.q: Orders arrive at {rate} per second. Each worker packs 1 per second, one worker per partition. What’s the minimum number of partitions?
min.why: {rate} records/s ÷ 1 record/s per partition = {rate} partitions. Teams usually add headroom on top.

reduce.q: Can you shrink the topic from 4 partitions back to 2?
reduce.no: No: partitions can only be added
reduce.empty: Only if the topic is empty
reduce.why: Kafka can only add partitions. To get fewer, you create a new topic and migrate to it.

maxConsumers.q: A topic has {n} partitions. At most how many consumers in ONE group can read it in parallel?
maxConsumers.why: {n}: each partition goes to one consumer in the group. Any extra consumers sit idle.

capacity.q: Producers write {p} records/s. One consumer handles {c} records/s. What’s the minimum number of partitions to keep up?
capacity.why: {p} ÷ {c} = {k} partitions, so {k} consumers can work in parallel.

unit.q: The unit of parallelism in Kafka is the…
unit.why: Partitions are what get spread across consumers (and brokers).

shrink.q: How do you lower a topic’s partition count?
shrink.cannot: You can’t: create a new topic and migrate
shrink.delete: Delete the last partitions one by one
shrink.why: Partition counts only go up. Plan ahead, or move to a new topic.

2-2.title: Same customer, same belt
2-2.summary: Keys keep each customer’s events in order.

brief.title: alice’s three orders
brief.body: alice ordered a phone (#1), then a case (#2), then cancelled the case (#3). They must be handled in that order. Today the producer ignores keys and deals records round-robin across the conveyors.

busy.title: P0 is busy
busy.body: A bulk import just dumped a pile of parcels onto P0. The robot works through each conveyor at the same pace.

rr.title: Send alice’s 3 orders
rr.body: Press the button three times and watch the Delivered list. In what order does alice’s stuff get handled?
rr.success: Uh-oh: #2 and #3 were handled before #1! Round-robin put them on different conveyors, and P0 was busy.

keys.title: The key keeps the order
keys.body: With a key, the partitioner sends every record of a customer to the same partition. One partition is read in order, so that customer’s events are handled in order, even when another conveyor is faster.
keys.breaks: order is only guaranteed per partition. Records with different keys on different partitions have no order between them.

keyed.title: Try again, with keys
keyed.body: Now carol sends 3 orders with her key. Watch the delivery list.

where.why: P{p}, like all of carol’s orders. Same key, same partition.

how.q: To keep each customer’s events in order, the producer should…
how.key: Use the customer id as the key
how.why: Same key → same partition → read in order.

rr.q: Records spread round-robin (or keyless) give you…
rr.why: They land on different partitions, which are read independently.

first.q: alice’s records sit at offsets {a}, {b} and {c} of P1. Which offset does a consumer read first?
first.why: A partition is read in offset order: {a}, then {b}, then {c}.

hot.q: One key gets 90% of all traffic. What happens?
hot.hotspot: Its partition becomes a hot spot
hot.why: All records of a key go to one partition, so one consumer gets swamped. That’s the hot key problem.

2-3.title: No label?
2-3.summary: Keyless records and the sticky partitioner.

brief.title: Keyless parcels ride together
brief.body: Not every event needs a key. With key = null, the default partitioner is sticky: it fills one partition’s batch, then moves to the next. Fewer, fuller batches mean fewer requests.
brief.breaks: real Kafka switches when the batch reaches batch.size bytes (16 KB by default). Here a batch is {b} parcels so you can see it.

fill.title: Watch the batches
fill.body: Six keyless parcels roll in. Notice they don’t alternate: they stick.

next.q: Where will the next keyless parcel go?
next.why: P{p}: the sticky partitioner keeps filling the current batch (up to {b} here) before switching.

why.q: Why stick to one partition instead of alternating on every record?
why.why: Sticky partitioning is a throughput optimization (KIP-794): full batches compress better and need fewer network round trips.

all.title: Fill every conveyor
all.body: Send keyless parcels until each conveyor has at least 4.
all.success: Even spread over time, and efficient batches along the way.

default.q: With the default partitioner, records with a null key are…
default.why: Keyless records stick to one partition per batch, then rotate.

count.q: Batches of {b} records, {n} partitions, starting at P0. You send {k} keyless records. How many land on P0?
count.why: P0 gets each batch number 0, {n}, 2·{n}… Counting {k} records in batches of {b}: {x} on P0.

why.why: Fuller batches mean fewer requests and better compression.

order.q: Do keyless records keep their order relative to each other?
order.partition: Only within the partition they land on
order.never: Never, not even within a partition
order.why: Order is per partition, so it holds only within each partition.

2-4.title: New belt, new chaos
2-4.summary: Adding partitions moves keys, and that breaks per-key ordering.

brief.title: The hub grows
brief.body: Business is booming and the team wants a 4th conveyor. Before pressing the button, remember what the partitioner computes: murmur2(key) % partitions.

before.title: Everyone in their place
before.body: Each customer sends an order. Note which conveyor each one uses.

same.q: After adding a 4th conveyor, will every customer still go to the same conveyor?
same.why: The divisor changed from 3 to 4, so hash % 4 differs from hash % 3 for many keys. Some stay, some move.

grow.title: Add the 4th conveyor
grow.body: Add P3, then send each customer again and spot who switched conveyors in the table.
grow.success: Some customers now live on a different conveyor, while their old orders stay where they were.

hurts.title: Why it hurts
hurts.body: Some of a customer’s old orders sit on one partition and the new ones on another. A consumer could handle the new ones first: per-key ordering broke at the resize.
hurts.breaks: plan partition counts up front. If you must grow a keyed topic, consider a new topic and a migration.

mod.q: A key’s (positive) hash is {h}. Which partition does it go to with 4 partitions?
A key’s (positive) hash is {h} and the topic has {n} partitions. Which partition?

risk.q: The main risk of adding partitions to a keyed topic is…
risk.ordering: Keys move, so per-key ordering breaks
risk.why: Existing records stay put, new ones may hash elsewhere, so a key’s history is split across partitions.

cmd.q: Which command adds partitions to a topic?
cmd.why: --alter --partitions raises the count. Reassign moves replicas between brokers.

old.moved: Are moved to the new partitions
old.why: Records are immutable and never move. Only new records use the new partition count.

3-1.title: Trucks wait or go
3-1.summary: Batching: batch.size and linger.ms trade latency for throughput.

brief.title: Every send is a trip
brief.body: Right now the producer ships every parcel on its own trip: one network request per record. Real producers group records per partition into batches. A batch leaves when it’s full (batch.size) or when it has waited linger.ms, whichever comes first.
brief.breaks: time is slowed down about 100× so you can see the trucks wait. Real linger.ms defaults to 5 ms (since Kafka 4.0), and batch.size is counted in bytes (16 KB), not parcels.

tune.title: Fewer trips, still fast
tune.body: Orders arrive 6 per second. Tune the two dials until you send ≤ 2.2 requests per second while parcels wait ≤ 700 ms on average, and hold it for 5 seconds.
tune.success: Fewer, fuller batches: less network chatter and only a little extra latency. That’s the batching trade-off.

when.q: batch.size = 4 parcels, linger.ms = 1000 ms, and parcels arrive at P0 one per second. After how many seconds does the first batch leave?
when.why: linger.ms runs out after 1 s, before the 4th parcel would arrive, so a partial batch leaves at second 1. Whichever limit comes first wins.

raise.why: Waiting a bit longer fills batches (better throughput and compression) at the cost of a little delay per record.

first.q: batch.size = {b} records, records arrive every {ms} ms to one partition, linger.ms = {L} ms. How many records does the first batch hold?
first.why: The batch closes when it’s full ({b}) or when linger.ms expires ({L} ms, by which time 1 + {L}/{ms} records could have arrived). Here that’s {count}.

linger.wait: How long to wait for more records before sending a batch
linger.retry: How long to wait between retries
linger.keep: How long records stay on the broker
linger.why: It’s a deliberate small delay so more records can join the batch.

default.q: What’s the default linger.ms in Kafka 4.x?
default.why: KIP-1030 changed it from 0 to 5 ms in Kafka 4.0, a small wait that improves batching.

bigger.tradeoff: Fewer requests and higher throughput, but more latency
bigger.why: Batching trades a little latency for a lot of efficiency.

3-2.title: Vacuum pack
3-2.summary: Compression: whole batches squeezed with gzip, snappy, lz4 or zstd.

brief.title: Squeeze the batch
brief.body: The network between the hub and the brokers is a narrow pipe. Producers can compress each batch before sending it. The broker stores it compressed, and the consumer unpacks it at the end.
brief.breaks: the ratios here are illustrative. Real compression depends on your data: repetitive JSON squeezes a lot, already-compressed images barely at all.

pipe.title: Fit through the pipe
pipe.body: 6 orders per second of 1 KB each, but the pipe only takes {cap} KB/s. Pick a codec that fits and watch the CPU cost.
pipe.success: It fits! Each codec trades CPU for size: zstd and gzip squeeze the most, lz4 and snappy are the fastest.

where.q: Where are the records finally decompressed?
where.why: The batch travels compressed end to end. The broker keeps it as the producer packed it (topic compression.type=producer), and the consumer decompresses.

best.why: More similar records in one batch means more repetition to squeeze. Batching and compression work together.

default.why: Compression is off by default. You opt in with compression.type.

unit.why: Compression applies to the whole batch, which is why bigger batches compress better.

broker.keeps: Stores the batch as the producer compressed it
broker.why: producer (the default) keeps whatever codec the producer used. No recompression.

wire.q: {rate} records/s of {kb} KB each, compressed to {pct}% of their size. How many KB/s go over the network?

3-3.title: Signed receipts
3-3.summary: acks: when does a write count as saved? Crash the leader and find out.

brief.title: Who signs the receipt?
brief.body: Each partition is copied to several brokers: a leader that takes the writes, and followers that copy from it. The producer’s acks setting decides when it gets its receipt: 0 (don’t wait), 1 (the leader wrote it), all (every in-sync replica has it).
brief.breaks: followers copy over the network. Here a copy takes about a second, so you can see the gap that real clusters close in milliseconds.

crash1.title: Crash test with acks=1
crash1.body: The producer sends three orders with acks=1 and then the leader’s broker dies. Watch the receipts.

fix.q: Receipts said ✓ but orders were lost. Which setting would have prevented it?
fix.why: With acks=all the producer only gets its receipt once every in-sync replica has the record, so a leader crash can’t take an acknowledged record with it.

crash2.title: Crash test with acks=all
crash2.body: Broker 2 is the leader now. First set acks=all, send a few orders, wait for their ✓, then crash the leader again. No acknowledged order should be lost.
crash2.success: Every ✓ survived the crash. That’s why acks=all has been the default since Kafka 3.0.

alone.q: Only one replica is left. With acks=all and the default min.insync.replicas=1, a write…
alone.succeeds: Succeeds: the leader alone is “all in-sync replicas”
alone.why: “All” means all in-sync replicas, and with min.insync.replicas=1 one is enough. Production clusters use RF=3 with min.insync.replicas=2. More in World 5.

one.q: acks=1 means the producer gets its ack when…
one.leader: The leader has written the record
one.why: Only the leader’s write is confirmed. Followers may not have it yet.

default.q: What’s the default acks since Kafka 3.0?
default.why: acks=all, together with idempotence, became the default in Kafka 3.0.

lose.q: Which setting can lose an acknowledged record if the leader dies right after acking?
lose.why: With acks=1 the record may exist only on the dead leader. (acks=0 can lose records too, but the producer was never promised anything.)

zero.nowait: The producer doesn’t wait for any acknowledgement
zero.why: Fire and forget: fastest, with no guarantee the record was stored.

3-4.title: Lost receipt
3-4.summary: Retries create duplicates, and idempotence stops them.

brief.title: The receipt got lost
brief.body: The network is flaky today. The broker writes the parcel, but the “got it!” reply sometimes vanishes on the way back. The producer can’t tell the difference, so it retries.
brief.breaks: Kafka doesn’t retry a fixed number of times: it keeps retrying until delivery.timeout.ms (2 minutes by default) runs out.

flaky.title: Flaky network
flaky.body: Send orders until something weird shows up on the conveyor.
flaky.success: A duplicate! The same order is on the log twice: the first write worked, only its receipt was lost.

seals.title: Numbered seals
seals.body: With idempotence, every producer gets an id and numbers its records per partition (seq). If a retry arrives with a number the broker already wrote, the broker drops it. Order is kept too, with up to 5 requests in flight. It’s on by default since Kafka 3.0.

fix.title: Turn on idempotence
fix.body: Switch idempotence on and keep sending. Watch the partitioner reject the retried copies.
fix.success: Retries still happen, but the log stays clean: each order exactly once.

protects.producers: Two different producers sending the same order
protects.why: It dedups retries from one producer session. Consumer-side duplicates and cross-producer duplicates need other tools (World 6).

default.q: What’s the default enable.idempotence since Kafka 3.0?
default.why: On by default, together with acks=all.

detect.q: How does the broker spot a duplicate retry?
detect.why: Each producer numbers its records per partition. A repeated number is a retry.

eos.session: Only for writes from one producer session into Kafka
eos.why: It removes producer-retry duplicates. End-to-end exactly-once needs transactions and read_committed consumers.

bound.q: What limits how long the producer keeps retrying?
bound.why: retries defaults to MAX_INT. delivery.timeout.ms (120 s) is the real bound.

review.title: Morning shift
review.streak: {n, plural, =0 {Start a streak today} one {# day streak} other {# day streak}}
review.score: {correct} of {total} remembered. Concepts you missed come back sooner.
review.emptyBody: Finish your first level and its concepts will start showing up here.
review.dueTitle: {n, plural, one {# concept} other {# concepts}} to refresh
review.dueBody: A few quick questions on things you learned a while ago, mixed together.
review.nextOn: Your next review is due on {date}.
review.why: Why bother? Recalling something just as you’re about to forget it is one of the most effective ways to make it stick (spaced retrieval practice).
